doc.title: Don Albert and Herbert Hall Interview, 1978-08-03

title: Jug bands, kazoo, washboards and string bands
summary: Jug bands only in New Orleans; Bob Burns's instrument came from there; Albert played mandolin, guitar and banjo.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Say what? What about, did you hear any jug players ever?
Only that in New Orleans. That's the only place. Uh-huh.

Would they be with name bands? No, no, no. We had them jug bands and guys playing them kazook things. And that was man. And it must be there. And they all up down the canal up down. Where they can house. And nickel the time. Washboards. Washboards. And the guy played that kazook thing. That's where Bob Burns got that from.
I don't know. That's all I know. No, the guy that, he played a bazooka like Bob Burns or whatever you want to call him.
No, no, Bob Burns got it from him. And Noon.

Jimmy Noon? No, no, this guy was Noon Johnson. He used to play one, but that's not him. Yeah, yeah. He was a blues singer, too. Well, he sang everything. He sang poppin' songs like those guys. I don't know. Sometimes I'd hear guys get together with, you know, three and four guitars. They would just sit around and play blues and one good second behind the other.
Yeah, right, right. I've seen that. You're the punter's age and it has a lot no players to do. No.
What about, did you ever see guitars and violin players and bass players and mandolin players get together?
Yeah. No, no, no, no. That I can't remember. I played all the instruments. I played the mandolin. I played the guitars and the banjoers, but not in a consolidated deal.
What do you mean by a string band?
A string band on strings is with these, Brian. Yeah. Yeah. And you didn't see that over there, huh?
